newsitem.title: HONG KONG: S&P says HK property prices seen remaining high.
newsitem.headline: S&P says HK property prices seen remaining high.

text.p: Standard & Poor's Corp said on Wednesday that demand for property in Hong Kong, particularly residential property, will continue to be very strong relative to supply after the territory's reversion to China, keeping property prices high relative to global standards.

The health of the property sector has an enormous impact on Hong Kong's economy, particularly the corporate, bank and government sectors, and many blue-chip companies are largely exposed to the local property sector, S&P said in a report.

Hong Kong's banks are sensitive to the property sector's performance due to their loan portfolios' exposure to real estate, while land sales and other property-related income are a significant source of revenue for the government.

Paul Coughlin, managing director of S&P's Hong Kong office, said demand for property in Hong Kong is affected by the growing population, the influx of Chinese-based companies, and decreasing average household size and increasing wealth.
A large portion of the population was in the home-buying bracket, and local culture emphasised home ownership, he said.
Coughlin said the high costs of property were driven by scarcity in supply.
Public housing accounts for 51 percent of the market. While only low-income households are eligible, tenants can remain in public housing no matter how wealthy they later become.
The supply of private sector housing has not been steady and has exhibited a downward trend in recent years, exacerbating the recent price escalation, S&P said.
The scarcity of prime, urban developable land also contributes to the imbalance between supply and demand, it said.

S&P said Hong Kong is one of the most densely populated areas in the world and its property market by global standards ranks as one of the most expensive, and the dynamics of the property market are unlikely to change in the near term.

Although the government has considerable interest in keeping land values high because of substantial revenues from land sales, from time to time it has attempted to stabilize the market by foreshadowing increased land supply, S&P said.
In addition, after the change in sovereignty, the Hong Kong government will no longer be constrained by Sino-British restrictions on the sale of government land, it added.

Influential figures in the incoming administration also seem keen on increasing the supply of land for housing, but it remains to be seen whether actions will be taken to slow the upward movement of the residential property market, S&P said.
